strengths: Clear and rigorously proven theoretical contributions with asymptotic improvements in two practical generation settings (O(K√L log L) for generation from scratch, O(L log L + K²) for generation with prompt)
Method is general and model-agnostic, applicable to any convolutional sequence model without retraining
Addresses a real and well-motivated problem: slow auto-regressive generation in convolutional models despite efficient training
Technical soundness with clearly described algorithms and correct proofs; clever use of FFT for batch precomputation
Simplicity and practical applicability of the core technique make it potentially implementable in existing systems
weaknesses: Critical: Experimental validation is severely limited—only synthetic CPU timing on a single layer, with no real language modeling tasks, actual model implementations, or end-to-end evaluation

No evidence that theoretical asymptotic improvements translate to wall-clock speedups on realistic systems with accelerators, batching, or modern inference frameworks; authors acknowledge inability to provide optimized timings

Practical limitations inadequately addressed: method requires knowing K (tokens to generate) in advance, breaking applicability to greedy/beam search; O(K²) dominates when K is large, potentially negating improvements
Limited novelty: core technique is a straightforward application of FFT precomputation; conceptual innovation is incremental rather than groundbreaking
Missing standard comparisons and ablations: no comparison with distillation approaches, SSM baselines, or deployed inference systems; no sensitivity analysis on cache size or K/L ratios

Incomplete practical analysis: no discussion of how per-layer improvements compose in stacked architectures, interaction with modern deployment techniques (continuous batching, paged attention), or characterization of scenarios where method helps vs. hurts
Online learning section (Section 4) feels disconnected from main narrative with no new learning-theoretic contributions, only inherited regret bounds
No code, reproducibility artifacts, or supplementary materials mentioned; no standard language modeling benchmarks

Well-presented algorithms with rigorous proofs and clear notation

Severe theory-practice gap: constant factors and hardware considerations completely unexamined; authors acknowledge difficulty presenting optimized timing results
Unclear practical applicability: no guidance on when FutureFill outperforms SSMs (which achieve O(1) per-token) or other alternatives
Missing experimental validation of claims: only vague anecdotal statement about 'inference gains' on accelerated hardware with no concrete evidence
Limited scope: applies only to convolutional models; no comparison to SSM inference or discussion of why practitioners would use this approach
Incomplete technical analysis: no multi-layer dynamics, batching effects, memory bandwidth costs, or numerical stability discussion
Lacks real-world workload validation: no language modeling experiments, no text generation tasks, only synthetic generation loops
No reproducibility: no code, minimal implementation details, toy-scale single-layer experiments preclude reproduction
Weak baseline comparisons: missing KV caching, modern inference optimizations, and the distillation approach of Massaroli et al. 2024

strengths: Clear and elegant algorithmic contribution: FutureFill primitive and associated algorithms provide intuitive and theoretically grounded improvements from O(L²) to O(L log² L) generation complexity
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with rigorous proofs and practical time-memory tradeoffs (Epoched-FutureFill vs. Continuous-FutureFill variants)
Thorough experimental validation with extensive ablations on generation length, model depth/width, cache size K, and both from-scratch and prompt-based generation scenarios
Demonstrated real speedups on realistic models (1.5-2× on 600-800M parameter models), showing theoretical gains translate to practice
Model-agnostic approach applicable to any convolutional sequence model (STUs, Hyena, etc.); works with both purely convolutional and hybrid architectures
Excellent presentation with clear exposition, well-designed visualizations, comprehensive appendices, and detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Modest practical speedup (1.5-2×) relative to theoretical complexity reduction suggests hardware/implementation factors significantly limit gains; benefits diminish at smaller generation lengths
Concurrent independent work [24] achieves identical O(L log² L) complexity via polynomial interpolation, reducing novelty; claimed simplicity advantage is subjective
Critical practical limitations not addressed: no support for quantization (standard in deployed LLMs); only applied to convolutional models in Transformer-dominated landscape

Experimental evaluation gaps: (1) no task-level evaluation (only raw speed), (2) random filter initialization rather than trained filters, (3) 'academic-sized' models only (unclear scaling to billion+ params), (4) single GPU only, (5) missing comparisons with alternative efficiency techniques (cache compression, sparse attention)
Cache size tuning underexplored: Epoched-FutureFill requires K=√(L log L) for optimality; guidance for adaptive K selection in variable-length scenarios is missing
Prefill performance underwhelming: Tables 5-6 show minimal improvement over baseline despite theoretical O(K) cache advantage, suggesting limited practical benefit for typical use cases

Algorithm 2 complexity: serialization of divide-and-conquer is non-intuitive; tracking k(t) as highest power of 2 dividing t adds implementation complexity without clear justification for this approach over alternatives

Limited model applicability validation: tested only on STU-based architectures; generalization to Hyena and other convolutional models claimed but not demonstrated; broader convolutional model ecosystem adoption unclear

strengths: Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs and clear FutureFill abstraction
Generality: applicable to any convolutional model without approximations or retraining
Multiple algorithmic variants offering practical time-memory tradeoffs

No requirement for model retraining or downstream architectural changes

Critical practical limitations: quantization not supported, yet standard in LLM deployment; insufficient batching analysis

Incomplete analysis: empirical cache optimization (Fig 2b) doesn't match theoretical prediction (Theorem 2); suggests large hidden constants or asymptotic analysis limitations

Missing crucial experiments: no profiling of where time is spent; no validation at extreme sequence lengths; no comparison on realistic batched inference; concurrent work [24] insufficiently differentiated
Cache and memory analysis incomplete: O(L) additional memory for Continuous-FutureFill not thoroughly compared; peak memory usage vs baselines missing

strengths: Clean and intuitive FutureFill primitive that elegantly decomposes convolutions, enabling efficient online computation with clear divide-and-conquer structure
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with multiple algorithmic variants offering practical time-memory tradeoffs (Epoched vs. Continuous), backed by rigorous proofs
Thorough experimental validation: controlled experiments confirm asymptotic complexity, extensive ablations across model architectures/sizes, multiple generation scenarios tested
General applicability to any convolutional model class (STUs, Hyena, etc.) independent of training procedure; handles both generation from scratch and with prompts
Addresses practically important scenario of cache size reduction from O(L+K) to O(K) when generating from prompts, with consistent 1.5-1.7× speedups demonstrated
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: asymptotic improvements (O(L²) → O(L log² L)) yield modest practical speedups (1.5-1.7×), with polylog factors and hardware effects substantially reducing theoretical benefits

Critical lack of downstream task evaluation: filters randomly initialized, no language modeling perplexity metrics, no end-to-end LLM generation quality assessment, limiting evidence of real-world impact
Does not address quantization, which is ubiquitous in production LLMs; dismisses approximate efficiency methods (KV cache compression) without empirical comparison despite their practical prevalence

Limited applicability to current LLM landscape: convolutional models not mainstream, experiments only on academic scales (≤826M params), no comparison with standard Transformer inference engines or SSMs

Insufficient baselines: Transformer comparisons only on tiny models (2-layer, 32-dim), missing comparisons with KV cache compression [34] and other cache optimization techniques, concurrent work [24] achieves identical complexity

Modest novelty: FutureFill insight, while elegant, is relatively straightforward once recognized; subsequent algorithms are standard divide-and-conquer applications; Proposition 1 is direct consequence of convolution definition
